attack_chain.action: Initial infection: User installs malicious package from PyPI.

HTTP POST requests to Discord webhooks or other C2 endpoints during package installation
file_indicators: setup.py containing references to VM artifacts (e.g., 'VMware', 'VirtualBox'), analysis tools (e.g., 'wireshark.exe', 'procmon.exe'), or Discord webhook URLs
Downloaded files named payload.exe or similar written to disk during installation
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP requests to Discord webhook endpoints (https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...)
Connections to suspicious domains such as wtfismyip.com for public IP checks
HTTP requests to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., http://malicious-server.com)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor package installation processes for anti-analysis checks in setup.py (such as VM artifact detection, username or public IP checks), unexpected network activity (especially HTTP POSTs to Discord webhooks or requests to suspicious domains), and the downloading/execution of binaries. Flag any setup.py scripts that reference VM artifacts, known usernames, or public IP checks, and alert on any HTTP POSTs to Discord or similar services during installation. Correlate file creation events for payload.exe or similar executables with installation events to identify malicious activity.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code queries Windows registry keys for driver and provider information, specifically looking for values associated with virtual machines such as VMware or VirtualBox, and terminates execution if virtualization is detected, further evading automated analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Registry checks for VM detection are a common anti-analysis technique in malware, used to avoid running in controlled environments.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not check for virtualization or exit based on registry values related to VM drivers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise software may check for virtualization for licensing or optimization, but not to evade analysis or self-terminate.
key_indicators: REG QUERY for VM-related drivers
winreg access to system registry keys
Conditional exit on detection of VMware/VBOX
Use of registry values to determine environment

package_info.why_malicious: The package is part of a large-scale, persistent campaign distributing Python malware via PyPI. It is designed to exfiltrate sensitive data, manipulate cryptocurrency transactions, tamper with applications, evade analysis, and disable system defenses. The malware evolves from plaintext to multi-layer obfuscation and encrypted payloads, with a focus on Windows systems.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes on import, performing environment checks to evade sandboxes and researchers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued execution only on real victim systems.

attack_chain.action: Silently installs dependencies and prepares for further actions.
Drops, decrypts, and executes secondary payloads using obfuscation and encryption.
Performs data theft: browser, application, Discord, gaming, and file exfiltration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data is collected and prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Manipulates cryptocurrency transactions by hijacking clipboard addresses.
attack_chain.leads_to: Redirection of cryptocurrency funds to attacker.

attack_chain.action: Tampers with applications (e.g., Exodus wallet) to inject further malicious code.
Disables system defenses, hides/deletes files, and exfiltrates data via multiple channels.

behavioral_signatures: Silent subprocess execution with CREATE_NO_WINDOW at import-time
Environment and VM detection with self-termination based on hardcoded lists and registry checks
Clipboard monitoring and replacement of cryptocurrency addresses using regex patterns

Dropping and executing encrypted/obfuscated payloads in APPDATA
Disabling system defenses via PowerShell commands
Hosts file manipulation to block security vendor domains
Multi-channel data exfiltration (file-sharing services, Discord webhooks, Telegram API)
Webcam and screenshot capture for data theft

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Python packages that execute subprocesses with CREATE_NO_WINDOW at import-time, perform environment or VM checks with self-termination, or contain obfuscated/encrypted code in __init__.py. Detect clipboard access patterns matching cryptocurrency addresses and unauthorized modification of application binaries, especially in cryptocurrency wallet directories. Watch for network connections to known malware infrastructure (bananasquad.ru, Discord webhooks, file-sharing services, Telegram API). Alert on PowerShell scripts disabling security features or hosts file modifications blocking security vendors. Correlate with file creation/deletion in APPDATA and hidden file activity, as well as webcam or screenshot capture attempts.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code queries the Windows registry for keys associated with virtual machine drivers (e.g., VMware, VirtualBox) and terminates execution if virtualization is detected, avoiding execution in analysis environments.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Registry checks for VM artifacts are used to evade sandboxes and automated analysis environments.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code should not evade analysis environments by detecting virtualization and self-terminating.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some software may check for virtualization for licensing or optimization, but not to evade detection.
key_indicators: Registry queries for VM drivers
Conditional exit on detection of virtualization
Hardcoded registry paths for VM detection

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are part of a coordinated, persistent campaign to deploy information-stealing malware. They exfiltrate sensitive data, manipulate cryptocurrency transactions, tamper with applications, evade detection, and disable system defenses. The attacker rapidly evolves techniques, using obfuscation, encryption, and multi-stage payloads to maximize impact and evade analysis.

attack_chain.action: Initial infection: User installs malicious package from PyPI.
Environment checks: Malware verifies it is not running in a sandbox or VM by inspecting directories, usernames, hardware IDs, system resources, and registry keys.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued execution if safe, self-termination if not

attack_chain.action: Payload decryption and execution: Encrypted or obfuscated payloads are decrypted and executed, enabling the main malicious functionality.
Data theft: Malware steals browser, application, file, and system data, including cryptocurrency wallet information.
Cryptocurrency address hijacking: Clipboard is monitored for cryptocurrency addresses and replaced with attacker-controlled addresses.
Application tampering: Exodus wallet is modified by overwriting app.asar with attacker-controlled code to enable further exfiltration.
Exfiltration: Stolen data is archived and sent to attacker-controlled endpoints via network connections.

behavioral_signatures: Hidden subprocess execution using CREATE_NO_WINDOW flag
Environment, sandbox, or VM detection and conditional self-termination
Clipboard monitoring and modification for cryptocurrency addresses using regex
Unauthorized modification of application files (e.g., Exodus app.asar)
Dynamic decryption and execution of secondary payloads at runtime
Multi-layered code obfuscation (base64, zlib, marshal, exec) at import-time
file_indicators: Unexpected writes to %APPDATA% or user directories
Modification or replacement of app.asar in Exodus wallet directory
Creation of .pyw or .py files with random or suspicious names in user directories
Presence of obfuscated or encrypted code blocks in __init__.py or other core package files
network_indicators: Outbound connections to bananasquad.ru, gofile.io, anonfiles.com, discord.com/api/webhooks
Exfiltration of data to file-sharing services or Telegram bot API endpoints
Use of hardcoded cryptocurrency addresses (BTC, ETH, Monero, ADA, Dash) in network payloads
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for hidden subprocess creation, especially with the CREATE_NO_WINDOW flag. Flag packages that perform environment or VM checks and self-terminate. Detect clipboard access patterns matching cryptocurrency address regexes and unauthorized clipboard modifications. Alert on unauthorized modification or replacement of application files such as Exodus app.asar. Scan for obfuscated or encrypted code blocks in package files, especially in __init__.py. Monitor outbound connections to known malicious domains and file-sharing services. Correlate clipboard hijacking activity with the presence of hardcoded cryptocurrency addresses in code or network traffic.
